html:
This bar covers the two Burmese dynasties that reunited and ruled Burma (Myanmar) after the fall of Pagan: the Taungoo dynasty, from about 1510 to 1752, and the Konbaung dynasty, from 1752 until Britain deposed the last king in 1885.

The Taungoo kings started from a small fort town and built the largest empire in Southeast Asian history. Bayinnaung, king from 1550 to 1581, conquered the Shan states, Lan Na, Manipur and Ayutthaya, using Portuguese mercenaries and guns. The empire fell apart soon after his death, but later Taungoo kings rebuilt a smaller, more stable state ruled from Ava.

In 1752 the Taungoo state collapsed under a Mon rebellion. A village chief, Alaungpaya, rallied resistance and founded the Konbaung dynasty. It was even more aggressive:

  • It sacked Ayutthaya in 1767.
  • It beat four Qing invasions from China between 1765 and 1769.
  • It took Arakan, Manipur and Assam, which put it on the border of British India.

That border brought ruin. Britain won the First Anglo-Burmese War (1824 to 1826) and took Arakan and Tenasserim; a second war in 1852 took Lower Burma with Rangoon. King Mindon ruled what was left from his new capital, Mandalay, and tried to modernise. In the third war, in 1885, British troops took Mandalay in a few weeks and sent King Thibaw into exile in India. Burma became a province of the British Raj, ending a monarchy that went back to Pagan. Modern Myanmar's borders largely follow the Konbaung conquests.
